text: Every quantum state you've worked with so far has been treated as fixed, a snapshot in time. Real qubits evolve continuously, and exactly one equation governs how. This lesson introduces it conceptually, without solving it.

The time-dependent Schrödinger equation says: i-h-bar times the rate of change of the state vector equals H applied to the current state. H, the Hamiltonian, is the operator that encodes everything about how a system changes — know H, and you know the system's entire future evolution. It's Hermitian, the same kind of operator from chapter 1's postulates, so its eigenvalues are the system's possible energies. This course won't solve this equation for real atoms — that's physics-major territory. What matters here is the structure.

The Schrödinger equation is linear: if two states are both valid solutions under the same H, any superposition of them is also a valid solution. This isn't a minor footnote — it's the single fact guaranteeing superposition survives time evolution instead of being destroyed by it. A system that starts in superposition stays in superposition, generally a different one, as it evolves. Only measurement collapses a state; ordinary time evolution is deterministic and linear, a completely separate process from measurement's probabilistic collapse.

This is the identical linearity property used directly in chapter 5's no-cloning proof — seeing the same structural fact show up in two different arguments isn't a coincidence. And here's the payoff for computing: every quantum gate you'll study is, physically, a snapshot of Schrödinger-equation evolution under some deliberately engineered Hamiltonian, applied for a precise duration. Gates aren't an abstraction layered on top of physics — they ARE physics, engineered to implement a chosen computation.
Next lesson makes this completely concrete: a fully verified numeric example of the actual evolution matrix, and exactly what it does to a qubit's state.
